description: This cluster consists of 158 coupled articles, representing 8593 total citations. It ranks first in terms of the number of publications and impact (i.e., total citations) (see Table 3). This cluster’s key themes included innovation, competitive advantage, entrepreneurship, CSR, and performance (see Fig. 8). The most influential work of this theme is by Bateman and Crant (1993), titled ‘The proactive component of organizational behavior: A measure and correlates’ with 1069 citations. This significant study presented the stable disposition features of proactive behavior and provided the field’s most widely used proactivity related construct (i.e., proactive personality initial scale). Hemingway and Maclagan (2004) study on ‘Managers’ personal values as drivers of corporate social responsibility’ ranks the second most cited article (TC: 559). They contend that the commercial imperative is not the sole motivator of socially responsible decision-making. They advocate for personal initiative in CSR policies that makes a difference in the organization (i.e., formulation, adoption, and implementation). The Aragon-Correa ´ (1998) study, which ranks third with 511 citations, explores the importance of proactive business strategies in relation to the natural environment. Other notable studies in the cluster include Burke and Logsdon’s (1996) article, which received 471 citations, and Parker’s (1998) article, which received 464 citations.

The second cluster consists of 155 total articles with 7448 total citations. It remains the second most impactful cluster in terms of total citations. The major themes presented in this cluster include job performance, career development, career success, career satisfaction, and personality (see Fig. 9). Parker et al.’s (2006) article on ‘Modeling the antecedents of proactive behavior at work’ is the most influential work (TC: 692). The authors add to the body of knowledge by demonstrating PP as a significant predictor of proactive work behavior, as well as the role of breadth self-efficacy and flexible role orientation in mediating these relationships. The work of Baer and Frese’s (2003) on ‘Innovation is not enough: Climates for initiative and psychological safety, process innovations, and firm performance’ ranks second in this cluster (TC: 601). In order to gain a competitive advantage, this study investigates the direct and indirect influence of two climate dimensions (e.g., initiative climate and climate for psychological safety) on two important firm performance measures, such as a change in return on investment and firm goal achievement. Crant’s (1996) ranks the article third, with a total citation count of 341, demonstrating a strong link between the PP scale and entrepreneurial intentions. Other significant works include, Thompson’s (2005), article with 300 citations, and Crant’s (1995), article with 119 citations.

The third cluster entails 147 total papers with 7286 total citations. The key research themes reflected in this cluster include job crafting, work engagement, personal initiative, proactive behavior, and job satisfaction (see Fig. 10). The most influential work in this cluster is Christian et al.’s (2011) article on ‘Work engagement: A quantitative review and test of its relations with task and contextual Performance’ (TC: 868). A meta-analysis review demonstrates the relationship between individual dispositional characteristics (e.g., proactive personality, conscientiousness, and positive affect) and work engagement and other job characteristics as a distal antecedent mediated by proximal constructs. Sonnentag’s (2003), article on ‘Recovery, work engagement, and proactive behavior: A new look at the interface between non-work And work’ is the second most impactful study (TC: 800). A multilevel design study found significant daily fluctuations in individual behavior and attitudes, with day-level recovery appearing to be positive for day-level job engagement, as well as day-level personal initiative and pursuit of learning during the following work time. Bakker et al. (2012), article on ‘Proactive personality and job performance: The role of job crafting and work engagement’ is the third most impactful document (TC: 296). According to this study, Individuals with a PP are more likely to engage in job crafting and are always looking for ways to improve their job resources. Other important studies include; Berg et al. (2010), cited 290 times

The fourth cluster comprises 135 articles with 7293 total citations. Key research themes appeared, including leadership, innovation, employee voice, and motivation (see Fig. 11). Griffin et al.’s (2007) study on ‘A new model of work role performance: Positive behavior in uncertain and interdependent contexts’ is the most impactful study in this cluster (TC: 844). It demonstrates the impact of supervisory and employee self-rating behavior on the sub-dimension of work role performance, where proactivity (self-reported) was found to be a positive predictor of two external measures of proactivity. Morrison’s (2011), study on ‘Employee voice behavior: Integration and directions for future research’ is the second most influential article (TC: 515). Morrison examines and integrates existing literature on employee voice, proposing various individuals and contextual factors that encourage voice behavior. Parker et al.’s (2010) article, which ranks third with 312 citations, proposes a distal antecedent (e.g., individual differences, contextual variations in leadership, work design, and interpersonal climate) as a stimulus for proactive motivational states, which are used to enhance the proactive goal process. Other influential works include Burris’ (2012), cited 243 times, and Chiaburu et al.’s (2011), cited 228 times.

The fifth cluster consists of 61 publications and 4467 total citations. Socialization, feedback seeking, information seeking, performance, and newcomers are the major themes appeared in this cluster (see Fig. 12). Crant’s (2000) article on ‘Proactive Behavior in Organization’ is the most impactful document (TC: 968). The study investigates individual and contextual factors (antecedents) that broadly captured the elements of proactive behavior (general and context-specific actions) to promote job performance and career success. Parker and Collins’ (2010) study on ‘Taking stock: Integrating and differentiating multiple proactive behaviors’ ranks the second most impactful study in terms of citations (TC: 610). This study offers three high order sets of proactive behavior (e.g., proactive work behavior, proactive strategic behavior, and proactive person-environment fit behavior) that count change in internal organization− voice, organization and its environment fit− issue selling, and the person organization-fit− feedback seeking. Ashford and Black’s (1996), article is the third most impactful article (TC: 426). This study investigates various techniques that can assist newcomers in gaining personal control during the initial socialization process, thereby improving their satisfaction and performance. Other influential studies include; Kammeyer-Mueller and Wanberg’s (2003), cited 260 times, and Wanberg and Kammeyer-Mueller, ’s (2000), cited 237 times.
